cues.text: Rome Before the Fire

By the early 60s, a small but growing Christian community existed in the capital of the Roman Empire, distinct in the eyes of Roman officials from the more familiar Jewish population, though still widely misunderstood.
Christians had until this point generally been left in relative peace by the imperial government, tolerated as an obscure sect rather than actively hunted.
St. Paul had arrived in Rome as a prisoner appealing to Caesar around AD 60, and the community he addressed in his Letter to the Romans was already established there.
This uneasy toleration ended abruptly in the summer of AD 64.
The Great Fire of Rome
On the night of July 18-19, AD 64, a fire broke out near the Circus Maximus and burned for over a week, destroying large sections of the city.

Ancient historians, including Tacitus and Suetonius , record that many Romans suspected the emperor Nero himself of having ordered the fire set, in part to clear ground for his planned palace, the Domus Aurea.
Facing public suspicion, Nero sought a scapegoat.
According to Tacitus's Annals , he settled on the Christians of Rome, a group already regarded with popular hostility and suspicion for their refusal to worship the Roman gods or the emperor.
The Persecution
Nero's agents arrested Christians throughout the city.
In Tacitus's account, an "immense multitude" was convicted — not primarily on the charge of arson, which few believed, but on the charge of "hatred of the human race."

The punishments were deliberately theatrical and cruel: Christians were sewn into the skins of wild animals and torn apart by dogs, crucified, or set alight as living torches to illuminate Nero's gardens at night.
Tradition holds that both St. Peter and St. Paul were martyred in Rome during this persecution — Peter crucified, by tradition upside down at his own request, and Paul, as a Roman citizen, beheaded.
Their martyrdoms are traditionally dated to the mid-to-late 60s.
Aftermath and Legacy

The persecution under Nero is regarded as the first state-directed action against Christians as such, distinct from the earlier, more localized hostility Christians had faced from Jewish authorities in Judea.

Though confined largely to the city of Rome, it established a precedent — the idea that the Christian name itself could be treated as a capital offense — that would recur intermittently over the following two and a half centuries.
Nero's own reign ended in AD 68, when he was declared a public enemy by the Senate and died by suicide.
But the persecution he unleashed left Rome at the center of Christian memory, sanctified by the blood of its two greatest Apostles.
It was the see that Peter and Paul had both led and died for, and the foundation of the Church's abiding reverence for the city as the seat of Peter's successors.
